environmentalPersistence: Low — oxidizes in air within hours to days; photodegradation rapid

lowDose.description: Mild defense priming, slight stomatal modulation, no visible morphological effects. Some evidence of insect repellence signaling at these concentrations.

highDose.description: Membrane disruption, oxidative stress, chlorosis, mild necrosis at prolonged high exposure, stomatal closure.

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Mild to moderate — terpenoid membrane effects slow cell division
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Mild downward curl — less pronounced than MeJA or ethylene
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Mild — some membrane disruption affects turgor
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Moderate — chloroplast membrane sensitivity to terpenoids
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Mild — only at prolonged high doses; primarily leaf margin browning
morphologicalEffects.pigmentation: Moderate anthocyanin induction — terpene-triggered defense response in Coleus
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Mildly inhibited at high doses — linalool is allelopathic
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Young leaves slightly more sensitive; effects relatively uniform

physiologyEffects.membranePermeability: Increased — terpenoids are lipophilic and disrupt bilayer integrity

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate — lipophilic membrane disruption generates ROS
molecularEffects.lipidPeroxidation: Moderate — membrane disruption is primary mechanism

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Moderate — linalool has well-documented antimicrobial properties
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Mixed — antimicrobial action affects both beneficial and pathogenic bacteria
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Antifungal activity — reduces both pathogenic and mycorrhizal fungi
microbiomeEffects.rhizosphereStability: Moderately disrupted via allelopathic root effects

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: 1–2 weeks — linalool degrades quickly; good recovery expected
temporalDynamics.sensitization: Mild priming — prior linalool exposure upregulates terpene response pathways

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → slightly deeper purple-green (anthocyanin); mild yellowing at high doses; leaf margins brown at prolonged exposure
visualSimulation.damageSpread: Uniform across leaf surface, margins last
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate purple glow — anthocyanin and linalool oxide metabolite signature
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Moderately reduced, slower; slight clustering — antimicrobial effect visible
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Good — fades back toward green within 1–2 weeks; minimal scarring

synergies.synergyNote: Linalool + MeJA or MeSA creates a strong terpene-jasmonate defense synergy — all three push pigmentation and defenseProteins axes simultaneously; observed in plant volatile blends under herbivore attack
synergies.antagonismNote: Linalool's mild defense priming can partially delay ethylene-driven senescence at low concentrations

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Lavender, coriander, basil, many flowering plants; major component of over 200 plant species' volatile blends
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Biopesticide research; natural insect repellent; flavor and fragrance industry
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Low — GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) for food use; mild skin sensitizer at high concentrations
educationalContext.climateLink: Terpene emissions from plants increase with temperature — linalool flux is a significant component of biogenic VOC emissions affecting atmospheric chemistry
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Both — major component of lavender essential oil widely used indoors; significant outdoor emission from flowering plants
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: The smell of lavender is linalool — students can connect a chemical they encounter daily to real plant defense biology and atmospheric chemistry
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Biogenic VOC emissions, atmospheric ozone formation, natural pesticide development
